objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why and how instructors assess learners, choose between traditional and authentic assessment, run a learner-centered debrief with maneuver and risk management grades, write good test items and oral questions, and deliver an assessment that a learner accepts and can act on.
why: Assessment gives the instructor immediate feedback on the quality of instruction, and it is how you guide a learner, suggest improvements and give positive reinforcement [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. As a CFI you are the only person who can decide a learner is ready for solo, and signing that endorsement or a practical test recommendation is a serious responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

prereading.label: AIH 6-1 to 6-5
prereading.what: Assessment terms, purpose, the eight characteristics of effective assessment, traditional assessment and the six characteristics of a good test.

prereading.label: AIH 6-5 to 6-9
prereading.what: Authentic assessment, learner-centered grading (replay, reconstruct, reflect, redirect), the maneuver and risk management rubrics, and choosing an assessment method.

prereading.label: AIH 6-10 to 6-13
prereading.what: Critiques, oral assessment, effective questions, questions to avoid and answering learner questions.

prereading.label: AIH 9-11 to 9-14
prereading.what: Assessment of piloting ability, postflight evaluation, solo supervision and practical test recommendations.

prereading.label: AIH B-1 to B-5
prereading.what: Writing test items: supply type, selection type, true-false, multiple choice and matching.

prereading.label: AIH 1-28
prereading.what: Assessing SRM skills: how to grade a learner's decisions, not just the maneuver.

prereading.label: AIH 10-2 to 10-4
prereading.what: The risk assessment matrix, and what a learner should be able to do in risk management at each phase of training.

warmup: Think first: after a flight your learner says, 'That went great, I didn't make any mistakes.' You saw two steep turns that lost 150 feet and a late checklist. How do you tell him, so that he believes you, remembers it, and knows exactly what to fix next time? And who should speak first in that debrief, you or him?

key_terms.def: Written testing such as multiple choice or matching, with one correct answer per item. It usually checks the rote and understanding levels of learning [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].
Assessment where the learner performs real-world tasks and generates a solution instead of choosing one, against criteria known in advance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].
A guide for scoring performance in a reliable, fair and valid way: dimensions to judge, a rating scale and standards for each level [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].
Diagnostic assessment checks knowledge or skill before a course. Formative is ungraded and wraps up one lesson. Summative measures progress so far, like a stage check [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].
Sympathy or over-identification with a learner that bends the instructor's objectivity [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].
How well a test measures what it is supposed to measure. It is the most important consideration in judging a test [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].
How consistent a test's results are when the measurement is repeated [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].
A learner self-assessment followed by a discussion that compares it with the instructor's assessment [[25:137|AIH 6-6]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

A test that measures performance against set criteria (standards). The ACS practical tests are criterion referenced because every successful applicant must meet the same high standards [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].
The top risk management grade: the learner gathers the key data, weighs options and their risks and decides, with no instructor intervention needed [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
In a multiple choice item, the stem is the question or problem; the wrong answers are distractors [[25:198|AIH B-2]].
An oral question about why or how that makes the learner analyze, solve problems and draw conclusions, as opposed to a fact question [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

chunks.title: What assessment is for, and the words that go with it

body.p: Assessment is an essential part of teaching and learning. It gives you immediate feedback on the quality of your instruction, and you use it all the time to guide the learner, suggest improvements and give positive reinforcement [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. Assessment of learning can happen before, during and after training [[25:106|AIH 5-3]].

Purpose of assessment. Both you and the learner need to know how well the learner is progressing. A good assessment gives practical, specific feedback with direction on how to raise the level of performance. Most important, it gives the learner a chance for self-evaluation, which builds aeronautical decision-making and judgment [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. It also shows you where to put more emphasis: if several learners stumble at the same step of a weight and balance problem, you need a better explanation, another demonstration or more emphasis there [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

head: Term
What it means
Flight school example
rows: Formal
Documented, such as a quiz or written exam, used periodically and at the end of a course to show whether objectives were met [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
A quiz or a written exam at the end of ground school [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
Informal
Happens as needed, can include verbal critique, and is not part of the final grade [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
Comments after each landing (application)
Diagnostic
Checks knowledge or skills before a course of instruction [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
Finding out what a transitioning pilot already knows (application)
Formative
Not graded. Wraps up the lesson, sets up the next one and tells you what to reinforce [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
The end-of-lesson debrief (application)
Summative
Used periodically to measure how far learning has progressed [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
A stage check, chapter quiz or end-of-course test [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]

callout.text: Application memory aid: Diagnostic is Day one, Formative is For next lesson, Summative is the Sum so far [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

check.q: Several of your ground school learners miss the same step of a weight and balance problem. What does the assessment tell you?
check.a: That you need a more detailed explanation, another demonstration of that step, or special emphasis on it in later assessments [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

body.p: To give direction and raise performance, an assessment has to be factual and line up with the lesson's completion standards [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. The AIH lists eight characteristics [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]:

head: Characteristic
What it means
What you do
rows: Objective

Based on the facts of the performance as they were, not as they could have been. Personal likes, dislikes and personality conflicts can bend it; over-identifying with a learner is halo error [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Grade the flight you saw, even for a learner you like
Flexible
Judge the whole performance in its context; good learners sometimes fly poorly and poor learners well [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Fit tone, technique and content to the occasion and the learner; decide what to say, omit, stress and minimize [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Acceptable
Learners must have confidence in your qualifications, teaching ability, sincerity, competence and authority; a certificate alone rarely does it [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Present it fairly, with authority, conviction and sincerity, from recognizable competence [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Comprehensive
Not necessarily long. Covers strengths and weaknesses in proportion to the situation [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Pick a few major points or several minor ones, whichever helps more [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Constructive
Pointless unless the learner benefits [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Pair every weakness with positive guidance; drop praise for its own sake and negative comments that point nowhere [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Organized
Any logical pattern the learner can follow [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Follow the sequence of the flight, work backward from the point of failure, or build around one glaring deficiency [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Thoughtful
Respects the learner's need for self-esteem, recognition and approval; no ridicule, anger or fun at the learner's expense [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Give criticism in private [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Specific
Learners cannot act on vague comments like 'your second weld was not as good as your first' [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Say why and how to fix it; at the end the learner knows what went well, what went poorly and how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]

callout.text: Application: before you debrief, write the one or two most important points on your kneeboard. It keeps the assessment organized, specific and comprehensive without becoming a list of every small error [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

check.q: Your favorite learner flies a sloppy pattern and you let it go because she is usually so good. Which characteristic did you break, and what is the error called?
check.a: Objectivity. Sympathy or over-identification that bends objectivity is called halo error [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

chunks.title: Traditional assessment and the characteristics of a good test

body.p: Traditional assessments are written tests such as multiple choice, matching, true/false and fill in the blank, done in a set time, with a single correct response per item [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. They assume all learners learn the same thing, rely on rote memorization and are often machine scored, so they show little of the learner's thought process [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Scored with simple scales like the ones below, a satisfactory grade on one lesson may not show the learner can apply the knowledge somewhere else [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

They still have a place. They check the learner's grasp of information, concepts, terms, processes and rules: the factual foundation needed to reach higher levels of learning [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Carefully written scenario questions can even assess higher levels [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

A test is a set of questions, problems or exercises to find out whether the learner has a knowledge or skill. Each test item measures a single objective and calls for a single response [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]. Effective tests share six characteristics [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]:

head: Characteristic
Meaning
rows: Reliability
Consistent results with repeated measurement. Remember that a learner may improve on a retake because the first test taught something [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Validity
Measures what it is supposed to measure; the most important consideration. Have several instructors read the test against the objectives and drop items that do not fit them [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Usability
Easy to give and grade: readable type, clear and concise directions and items, clear graphics [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Objectivity
Singleness of scoring. Essays are hard to grade objectively; true/false and multiple choice are much easier [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Comprehensiveness
Samples a proper cross-section of the objectives, like checking compression on every cylinder, not just one [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Discrimination
Tells learners apart: a wide range of scores, all levels of difficulty, and items that separate levels of achievement. Minimum standards matter far more for pilot certification [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]

callout.text: Teaching to the test is a trap. Test preparation materials stress rote learning, the lowest level, and examiners report applicants who passed the knowledge test easily but showed a lack of knowledge in the oral. Use them only as a supplement to instructor-led training [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

check.q: A presolo quiz includes questions on airline dispatch rules your learner will never use. Which test characteristic suffers most?
check.a: Validity. Items that do not pertain directly to the course objectives should be modified or eliminated [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

body.p: Good test items are hard to write, so many instructors use commercial test materials; some keep their own bank of items [[25:197|AIH B-1]]. If you write your own, know the two families [[25:197|AIH B-1]]:

head: Item type
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: Supply type (word, sentence or paragraph answer)
Lets the learner organize knowledge and express ideas; useful on a presolo test to check knowledge of procedures [[25:197|AIH B-1]]
Cannot be graded reliably, and takes longer to answer and to grade [[25:197|AIH B-1]]
Selection type (pick from alternatives)
Highly reliable, can be machine scored, compares learners and classes, and covers many areas in a short time [[25:197|AIH B-1]]
Relies on rote memorization and assumes everyone learns the same thing [[25:197|AIH B-1]]
True-false
Good for facts and details with only two possible answers [[25:198|AIH B-2]]
Greatest probability of guessing; tends to test rote memory, so generally not considered valid [[25:198|AIH B-2]]
Multiple choice
More widely used and versatile than matching or true/false; can test from facts up to reasoning and application [[25:198|AIH B-2]]
Hard to write a clear stem, an answer that cannot be refuted and attractive distractors [[25:199|AIH B-3]]
Matching
Measures many samples of knowledge quickly and tests relationships between terms; reduces guessing [[25:201|AIH B-5]]
If the lists split into obvious groups, it turns into several easy multiple choice items [[25:201|AIH B-5]]

body.p: Multiple choice tips from the AIH: use three or four alternatives, since more than four convincing ones is hard to write [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. Use common learner errors as distractors [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. Prefer a question stem over an incomplete sentence [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. Keep each item independent of the others, emphasize any negative word, and avoid double negatives and trick questions [[25:200|AIH B-4]]. Watch the length of the correct answer: research found the correct alternatives on instructor-made tests tend to be longer than the wrong ones [[25:201|AIH B-5]].
The item above breaks three stem rules: it carries irrelevant information, its negative needs emphasis, and the 'a' at the end of the stem does not fit every choice [[25:200|AIH B-4]].

check.q: Why does the AIH call true-false items generally not valid?
check.a: They have the greatest probability of guessing and are more likely to test rote memory than knowledge of the subject, so they do not measure what they are meant to measure [[25:198|AIH B-2]].

body.p: Authentic assessment asks the learner to perform real-world tasks and generate responses rather than pick from set answers. With open-ended questions and set performance criteria, it focuses on the learning process, builds real-world skills, encourages higher order thinking and teaches learners to assess their own work [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. It checks the application and correlation levels, not just rote and understanding, and the learner knows the criteria in advance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

Learner-centered assessment. The first part of authentic assessment is a 'collaborative critique', a form of learner-centered grading. You use a four-step series of open-ended questions to guide the learner through a complete self-assessment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]:

head: Step
What happens
Sample prompt
rows: Replay
The learner talks through the flight. You listen for places where the account seems off and discuss them at the right moment. It shows you the learner's judgment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
'Walk me through the flight from engine start.' (application)
Reconstruct
The learner names the key things they would have, could have or should have done differently [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
'What would you do differently on that second approach?' (application)
Reflect
The learner gives the events meaning [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
'What was the most important thing you learned today? How did you do compared with the ACS?' [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Redirect
The learner ties today's lessons to other experiences and future flights [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
'What personal minimums should you set, and what more practice might help?' [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]

body.p: Then you compare your assessment with the learner's in an in-depth discussion, and together you decide the learner's progress, which may be recorded on a rubric [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Collaborative assessment has two parts: learner self-assessment and a detailed assessment by the instructor [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

callout.text: Teach the learner to do it. A learner who has never self-assessed may be reluctant, so you may need to coach them into it [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. The PHAK calls a good post-flight analysis an often overlooked tool: review the flight objectively, then recognize, analyze and learn from the mistakes [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]].
The four R's run in time order: Replay what happened, Reconstruct what should have happened, Reflect on what it means, Redirect it to the future [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

check.q: During the replay your learner says the approach was stable. You saw the airspeed 15 knots fast at 300 feet. What do you do?
check.a: Note the discrepancy and discuss it with the learner at the right moment. Replay lets the learner check their own perceptions and gives you insight into their judgment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

body.p: Learner-centered grading uses two broad rubrics: one for skill-focused maneuvers or procedures, and one for single-pilot resource management (SRM), the decision-making side of flight training [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
Maneuver or procedure grades. At the end of a scenario the learner earns one of these [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]:

head: Grade
At the end of the scenario, the learner...
rows: Describe
Can describe the physical characteristics and cognitive elements of the activity but needs help to do it [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Explain
Can also explain the underlying concepts, principles and procedures, but still needs help to do it [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Practice
Can plan and execute the scenario; your coaching, instruction or help corrects the deviations and errors you identify [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Perform
Does it without help, finds and corrects own errors quickly, and successful completion is never in doubt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Not observed
Any event not done or not required [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]

body.p: Why explain matters: on a calm day a learner who can only describe a landing may land with some success at the rote level, but a gusty crosswind needs a deeper understanding. A learner who can explain the physics of lift, drag and crosswind correction is more likely to practice well and later perform under many conditions [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

The AIH example: after the flight, Linda asks Brian to self-assess with the four R's. Brian rates himself Perform because he made no mistakes; Linda rates him Practice. Talking it through, Brian sees where he needs more practice [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. The advantages: the learner takes part and builds the habit of honest self-assessment, and the grades describe a level of performance rather than prestige like A+, so the learner cannot flunk a lesson [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

callout.text: Do not force the rubric into an A to F mold. Grades should progress: a task might be a describe item on flight one, a practice item by flight three and a manage-decide item by flight five [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

check.q: Your learner flies slow flight well but you had to talk her back onto altitude twice. Which grade fits?
check.a: Practice: she can plan and execute it, but your coaching corrected the deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Perform needs no coaching and the learner corrects her own errors [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

body.p: A learner's performance is often assessed only on a technical level. For SRM you assess differently: how did the learner reach the decision, what resources were used, was risk assessed accurately at the go/no-go point, was situational awareness kept in the pattern, was workload managed, and how did they handle stress and fatigue [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]? SRM is about gathering information, analyzing it and making decisions, which is harder to learn than a specific maneuver [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]].
Assessing risk management skills. The SRM rubric has three grades [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]:

head: Grade
What the learner shows
rows: Explain
Can identify, describe and understand the risks in the scenario out loud, but must be prompted to identify risks and make decisions [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Practice
Identifies, understands and applies SRM to the real flight. Coaching quickly corrects minor errors. The learner is an active decision maker [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Manage-Decide

Gathers the most important data inside and outside the flight deck, identifies courses of action, evaluates the risk of each and decides. No instructor intervention is needed for a safe flight [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]

body.p: A typical path: the learner describes basic SRM on the first flight, later explains how it applies to scenarios on the ground and in the air, and earns manage-decide when quality decisions start coming from good SRM [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Give learners real decisions to grade: let them decide what to do about a preflight discrepancy first, assess a tailwind runway offered by the tower, or make the go/no-go call on the weather before each flight, while the final choice to fly stays with you [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Plan SBT lessons with simulated emergencies or heavy workload to test whether SRM is being applied [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

Tools you can watch them use. PAVE sorts hazards into pilot, aircraft, environment and external pressures [[30:11|RMH 1-2]]. The risk matrix rates each risk by likelihood and severity [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]:

What to expect by phase [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]: by first solo the learner can do a basic risk management analysis; after solo they analyze each planned flight with occasional coaching, you review the analysis for every solo flight, and they debrief you on its risk management afterward; on cross-countries they do a full risk analysis for every flight, which you review and approve like their other calculations.

callout.text: A numerical FRAT score can hide one extreme risk, such as a line of embedded thunderstorms, that the list does not weigh properly. Grade the learner's reasoning, not just the score [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

check.q: Your learner lists the risks of tonight's flight well but only acts on them when you ask, 'So what will you do about that?' Which SRM grade is she at?
check.a: Explain: she can identify and describe the risks but has to be prompted to identify risks and make decisions [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

body.p: To decide how to assess, the AIH gives a four-step process that works for the cognitive and affective domains and also for psychomotor skill testing. It goes from general to specific [[25:138|AIH 6-7]] [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

head: Step
What you do
AIH example (engine compression test)
rows: 1. Determine level-of-learning objectives
State a general objective at one learning level of one domain; it defines the scope [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]
'Describe how to perform a compression test' is an understanding-level objective [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]
2. List indicators of desired behaviors
Choose measurable behaviors that best show the objective was met; sample them, since you cannot measure everything [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
Answers should cover tools, setup, safety procedures and the steps to get readings [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
3. Establish criterion objectives
State the behavior, the conditions and the criteria to meet; good performance-based lesson objectives already do this [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
'Complete a quiz with a minimum passing score of 70 percent' [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
4. Develop criterion-referenced test items
Write items that measure the behaviors in the criterion objective; missed items show what was not covered well [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
Questions cover every area needed to show understanding of the procedure [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]

body.p: Matching method to stage. Authentic assessment may be less useful than traditional assessment early in training, because the learner does not yet know enough to take part fully. Once learners can analyze, synthesize and evaluate, they can participate more fully [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]. Make your own tests to measure progress: a presolo test should cover the regulations, local area, aircraft type and procedures, and a test of readiness for the knowledge test should draw on every lesson given [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. For the presolo test the rule is specific: you give it, and at the end you review every incorrect answer with the student before authorizing solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87]].

Performance testing fits training that involves an operation, procedure or process. You do not give the practical test, but you prepare the learner for it, so evaluate each element of the practical test before sending the applicant [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. The ACS practical tests are criterion referenced: every successful applicant must meet the standard [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Your evaluation of all the tasks need not be formal, but it should follow criterion-referenced testing [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

check.q: What three things does a criterion objective state?
check.a: The behavior expected, the conditions under which it is performed, and the criteria that must be met [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

body.p: A critique is an instructor-to-learner assessment used with either traditional or authentic assessment, one on one or in a class [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Its purpose is to improve the performance, so it must not become a chance to be overly critical. An effective critique looks at good and bad performance, the individual parts, how they relate and the overall performance, and it is as varied as the performance itself [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. It can be oral, written or both, and belongs right after the performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

head: Type
How it works
Watch out for
rows: Instructor/learner critique
You lead a group discussion and invite class members to critique [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Keep it controlled and organized, not a random free-for-all [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Learner-led critique
A learner leads; you may set the pattern or leave it to them [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
May not be efficient, but builds interest and learning [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Small group critique
Groups each analyze one area and report; together they make a comprehensive assessment [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Give them the criteria and guidelines [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Individual critique by another learner
Another learner presents the whole assessment, or you ask several learners about the performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Keep firm control of the process [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Self-critique
The learner critiques their own performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Still under your control and supervision [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Written critique
More time and thought, a permanent record, and every learner's comments for the performer [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
The rest of the class does not benefit [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]

body.p: Whatever the type, you resolve disagreements, correct wrong impressions, allow for the learners' inexperience, and save time at the end for anything left out, under-emphasized or worth repeating [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. A critique before the whole class can help everyone, but avoid embarrassing the learner who performed [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

check.q: What is the one disadvantage the AIH gives for a written critique?
check.a: Other members of the class do not benefit from it [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

chunks.title: Oral assessment and characteristics of effective questions

body.p: Oral assessment, direct or indirect questioning by the instructor, is the most common means of assessment [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Fact questions rely on memory and ask who, what, when and where. HOTS questions ask why or how and make the learner combine facts with analysis and problem solving [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].
Good questioning does a lot at once [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]:

bullets: Reveals how effective your teaching methods are.
Checks retention and comprehension of what was learned.
Emphasizes the important points, and finds the points that need more emphasis.
Promotes active participation, which is important to effective learning.

body.p: Characteristics of effective questions. Write pertinent questions in advance, for example in the lesson plan, and add impromptu ones as the lesson goes [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Objective questions have one correct answer; open-ended HOTS questions have many possible solutions [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. The AIH gives five rules for an effective question [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. The rules are the AIH's; the example questions are application:

head: Rule
Weak question
Better question
rows: Apply to the subject of instruction
In a run-up lesson: 'What is the speed limit in Class B airspace?'
'What did the RPM drop on the left mag tell you?'
Be brief and concise, but clear and definite
A rambling paragraph
'Why do we check carburetor heat during the run-up?'
Fit the learner's ability, experience and stage of training
Asking a 5-hour learner about icing certification
Asking about the run-up items they used today
Center on only one idea (who, what, when, where, how or why, not a mix)
'What do you do at the hold short line, and why?'
'Why do we stop at the hold short line?'
Present a challenge
'Is the fuel selector on BOTH?'
'What would happen if the selector were left on LEFT for the whole flight?'

callout.text: In the airplane, a learner telling you the next step before doing it is a quick oral assessment. The AIH uses the learner tells, learner does step to separate a misconception from a simple lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Why is 'How and when do you use carburetor heat?' a weak question?
check.a: It combines two ideas. An effective question centers on only one idea: who, what, when, where, how or why, not a combination [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

chunks.title: Questions to avoid, and answering learner questions

body.p: Types of questions to avoid. Effective quizzing leaves out yes/no questions like 'Do you understand?' or 'Do you have any questions?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Also avoid these [[25:142|AIH 6-11]] [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. For the first four the AIH gives only an example, so the 'What it is' wording there is this lesson's reading of that example (application):

head: Type to avoid
What it is
AIH example
rows: Puzzle
Piles on so many conditions it becomes a riddle
A tailwheel airplane with a weak right brake swerving left in a right crosswind during a full flap, power-on wheel landing [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Oversize
Far too broad to answer
'What do you do before beginning an engine overhaul?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Toss-up
Forces a choice between two things that may both be right
'Should you squawk 7700 or pick a landing spot?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Bewilderment
A confusing, wandering question
A long altimeter question mixing station pressure, temperature, warm fronts and mountains [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Trick question
Makes learners feel they are in a battle of wits with you, and the point of the lesson is lost [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Options 1, 2, 3, 4 listed as A. 4, B. 3, C. 2, D. 1 [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Irrelevant question
Brings in unrelated facts and slows progress [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]
Tire inflation on a test about magneto timing [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]

body.p: Answering learner questions. The AIH gives three tips [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]:

bullets: Be sure you clearly understand the question before you answer.
Show interest in the question and answer as directly and accurately as you can.
After you answer, find out whether the learner is satisfied.

body.p: If the full answer would bring in more than the learner needs at this point, say it is a good, pertinent question, explain that a detailed answer now would complicate the learning, and invite them to ask again at the right point in training [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. If you do not know, admit it freely, and promise to get the answer or help the learner look it up [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

callout.text: Bluffing an answer costs you the confidence in your competence and sincerity that makes your assessments acceptable to the learner [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

check.q: A presolo learner asks how a constant-speed propeller governor works. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Tell them it is a good, pertinent question, explain that a detailed answer now would unnecessarily complicate the learning, and invite them to ask again at the right point in training [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

body.p: Assessment of piloting ability shows how, what and how well a learner is learning, and it should give direction to raise performance. The learner must understand its purpose or will not accept it, and little improvement follows [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Flight instructors generally use the review, collaborative assessment (LCG), written tests and performance-based tests [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Reteaching. An assessment can also be a tool for reteaching. If you see a deficiency that needs it, demonstrate the maneuver, let the learner practice it under direction, then evaluate by watching the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Demonstrated ability. Base it on established standards of performance, adjusted for the learner's experience and stage of development, and judge mastery of the elements of the maneuver rather than just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Solo needs consistent proficiency on a number of maneuvers, and you should verify learners meet the proficiency requirements before any stage check [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

Postflight evaluation. Keep the learner informed of progress, maneuver by maneuver or in the postflight critique, and use written notes so you cover everything you saw [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Traditional scales like 'excellent, good, fair, poor' meet the instructor's needs but often not the learner's; after an SBT scenario, use collaborative assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In the demonstration-performance evaluation phase you record the performance, tell the learner the progress, give concrete suggestions and, if possible, avoid ending on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

Solo and the practical test. Debrief right after a solo, while the flight is vivid [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Before a solo endorsement, require consistent ability on all the fundamental maneuvers; supervising solo is by far your most important responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. A practical test recommendation should never rest on less than the complete procedure in the ACS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. The endorsement certifies the applicant received and logged training within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, is prepared, and has shown satisfactory knowledge of the areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39]].

callout.text: Signing off a learner who is not proficient for solo, or a pilot who does not meet the rules for a rating, is a serious deficiency the FAA may hold you accountable for, and a breach of faith with the learner [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

check.q: A learner flies a good landing, but you notice the flare came from a lucky gust and the airspeed control was poor. How should you judge it?
check.a: On mastery of the elements of the maneuver, not merely the overall result, against standards adjusted to his stage of training [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: Delivering an assessment badly can undo it. The risk is a learner who rejects your feedback, loses confidence or motivation, or leaves without knowing what to fix. The main hazards and the source-backed fixes:

head: Hazard
What can happen
Mitigation
rows: The learner does not know why you are assessing
They are unlikely to accept it, and little improvement follows [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Explain the purpose and the criteria up front; today's learners want to know the criteria they are assessed by [[25:144|AIH 6-13]]
Bias or halo error
An assessment that is not honest or factual [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Grade the performance as it was, not as it could have been [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Ridicule, anger or public criticism
Loss of self-esteem and dignity [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Respect feelings; criticize in private; in class, avoid embarrassing the performer [[25:134|AIH 6-3]] [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Vague or unbalanced comments
The learner cannot act on them [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Be specific; pair weaknesses with positive guidance; skip empty praise [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Ending on a sour note
A discouraged learner (application)
If possible, avoid ending the evaluation on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]
Self-assessment sprung on an untrained learner
Reluctance to take part [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]
Teach the learner how to take an active part [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]
Authentic assessment too early
The learner lacks the knowledge to participate [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]
Use more traditional assessment until the learner can analyze and evaluate [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]

body.p: Safety is part of delivery too. An unprepared learner is a serious hazard, so a syllabus, quality ground instruction and a thorough briefing before each flight are part of risk mitigation [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. An honest assessment before solo or a checkride is what keeps an unready learner on the ground [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

callout.text: Application: open the debrief by asking for the learner's self-assessment, agree on what went well, then give one or two specific fixes and close with the plan for next lesson. Every step comes from the characteristics and the learner-centered process above [[25:134|AIH 6-3]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

check.q: Why must the learner understand the purpose of an assessment?
check.a: Otherwise they are unlikely to accept the evaluation, and little improvement will result [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

body.p: These are instructor errors in assessing learners, built from what the sources warn about. Expect the examiner to role-play a learner and watch for them.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Asking 'Do you understand?'
The learner says yes and you learn nothing [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Ask a one-idea why or how question instead [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Grading only the maneuver
No idea how the learner made decisions [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Ask how they decided, what resources they used and how they assessed the risk [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Turning the rubric into A to F
Learner fixates on a grade [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]
Treat grades as progressive levels of performance [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]
Talking first in the debrief
The learner never builds self-assessment habits [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]
Replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect, then compare [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
A list of every small error
Overload, nothing remembered (application)
Choose a few major points or several minor ones, whichever helps more [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Only teaching to the test
Passes the knowledge test, struggles in the oral [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]
Use test prep only as a supplement to instructor-led training [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]
Signing a recommendation on a partial check
An applicant who is not ready
Require the full ACS procedure before you sign [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]
Bluffing an answer
Lost credibility [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Admit it and look it up together [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]

callout.text: Application: on the checkride, say the method out loud, for example 'I am using learner-centered grading because this learner can now analyze his own flight.' The AIH ties authentic assessment to a learner who can analyze, synthesize and evaluate [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

check.q: Your learner rated himself Perform and you rated Practice. What should the discussion produce?
check.a: An understanding of where he needs more practice before he reaches Perform, as in the AIH's Brian and Linda example [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

scenario.title: The debrief that went sideways
scenario.setup: Maya is a private pilot learner with 35 hours, two lessons from her solo cross-country. Today's scenario flight went to a nontowered airport 30 miles away. She flew the trip well, but at the destination she accepted a downwind landing because 'that's the runway everyone was using', and her short-field approach was 10 knots fast. Her previous instructor graded every lesson 'Satisfactory' and always started debriefs with a list of errors. Maya walks in and says, 'Just tell me if I passed.' Two other learners are waiting in the lobby for you.

questions.q: How do you open the debrief?
questions.a: With learner-centered assessment: ask Maya to replay the flight, reconstruct what she would change, reflect on what she learned and redirect it to future flights [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. She may need coaching because she has not self-assessed before [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

questions.q: How do you answer 'Did I pass?'
questions.a: Explain that the grades describe a level of performance, not prestige, so she cannot flunk a lesson; she shows a level of flight and SRM skill [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Make sure she understands the purpose of the assessment, or she is unlikely to accept it [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

questions.q: What maneuver grade might the short-field approach earn, and why?
questions.a: Likely Practice if your coaching was needed to correct the speed; Perform needs no coaching and the learner corrects her own deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Judge the elements, not just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

questions.q: How do you assess the downwind landing decision?
questions.a: With the SRM rubric: did she gather the key data, weigh the options and their risks and decide? Ask how she decided and what resources she used [[25:32|AIH 1-28]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Application: following other traffic without weighing the risk points to the Explain or Practice level, not Manage-Decide.

questions.q: Two learners are in the lobby. Where do you hold the debrief?
questions.a: In private. A thoughtful assessment respects the learner's feelings and gives criticism in private [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

Exactly what she did well, what she did poorly and specifically how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]], plus the plan for next lesson, since a formative assessment sets the stage for the next lesson [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

skills.do: Use appropriate methods and techniques to assess learner performance in ground or flight training (ACS FI.I.D.S1). The examiner sees you pick a method that fits the learner's stage, ask one-idea questions, run a learner-centered debrief that grades both the maneuver and the risk management, and deliver it so the learner knows what to fix.
skills.practice: Fly with a friend as your 'learner', then run the four-step debrief out loud [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] and rate the maneuver and SRM on the AIH rubrics [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Write five oral questions for one lesson and check each against the five rules for effective questions [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

quiz.q: Which type of assessment is ungraded, wraps up the lesson and tells you what to reinforce?
quiz.why: Formative assessments are not graded, wrap up the lesson and set the stage for the next one [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

quiz.q: An assessment that respects the learner's self-esteem and is given in private shows which characteristic?
quiz.why: A thoughtful assessment respects the learner's need for self-esteem; criticism should be given in private [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

quiz.q: Which characteristic of a test is called the most important?
quiz.why: Validity, the extent to which a test measures what it should, is the most important consideration [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

quiz.q: Which item type cannot be graded with reliability?
quiz.why: Supply-type items cannot be graded reliably; different graders may give different scores [[25:197|AIH B-1]].

quiz.q: Which maneuver grade means the learner can explain the concepts and procedures but still needs help to do it?
quiz.why: Explain: the learner understands the underlying concepts, principles and procedures but needs assistance to execute [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

quiz.q: What is the highest SRM grade in the AIH rubric?
quiz.why: The risk management rubric runs explain, practice, manage-decide [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

quiz.q: What is the first step in choosing an effective assessment method?
quiz.why: The four steps start with determining level-of-learning objectives [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

quiz.q: In which critique does a learner lead the assessment?
quiz.why: In a learner-led critique the instructor asks a learner to lead the assessment [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

quiz.q: What kind of question asks who, what, when or where and relies on memory or recall?
quiz.why: Fact questions are based on memory or recall and usually concern who, what, when and where [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

quiz.q: Which is one of the AIH's three tips for answering a learner's question?
options: Answer with as much advanced detail as you can
Save every question for the end of the lesson
After answering, find out whether the learner is satisfied with the answer
Turn every question back to the rest of the class
quiz.why: The three tips: be sure you understand the question, show interest and answer as directly and accurately as you can, then find out whether the learner is satisfied [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's landings earned 'Satisfactory' on every lesson, yet he cannot adapt to a gusty crosswind. What weakness of traditional grading does this show?
options: A satisfactory grade may not show the learner can apply the knowledge in a different situation
It takes too long to score
It measures only the affective domain
final_quiz.why: With traditional grading matrices, a satisfactory grade for one lesson may not reflect the ability to apply knowledge in a different situation [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. A learner who can explain the crosswind physics is more likely to adapt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: You give the same presolo test to a learner twice and her score rises. What does the AIH say about this?
options: The first test can serve as a learning device, so scores may improve
final_quiz.why: Knowledge and understanding can improve on later attempts at the same test, because the first test serves as a learning device [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner can plan and fly steep turns to ACS standards with no coaching and catches his own altitude drift. Which grade?
final_quiz.why: Perform: the learner does it without assistance and identifies and corrects errors and deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Manage-decide is an SRM grade, not a maneuver grade [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a cross-country, your learner notices fuel burn is higher than planned, checks the options, weighs the risk of each and diverts for fuel without any prompting. Which SRM grade fits?
final_quiz.why: Manage-decide: the learner gathers the most important data, identifies courses of action, evaluates their risk and makes the decision with no instructor intervention [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the debrief, your learner says, 'I'd set a higher crosswind limit for myself next time.' Which step of learner-centered assessment is this?
final_quiz.why: Redirect relates the session to future flights; one of its questions is what personal minimums should be established [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: Ten days into training, your learner knows few aviation concepts. Why might authentic assessment be a poor fit right now?
options: It is not allowed under part 61
The learner lacks the knowledge to participate fully in it
It cannot be used in the airplane
It only works in a classroom
final_quiz.why: Authentic assessment may not be as useful as traditional assessment early in training, because the learner does not have enough information to participate fully [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement is a criterion objective?
options: Describe how to perform a compression test
The learner will show understanding of compression tests by completing a quiz with a minimum passing score of 70 percent
List the tools used in a compression test
final_quiz.why: A criterion objective states the behavior, the conditions and the criteria; the 70 percent quiz is the AIH example [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. 'Describe how to perform a compression test' is the level-of-learning objective [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your ground school class critiques a mock briefing, and the discussion turns into everyone talking over each other. What did you fail to do?
options: Keep the instructor/learner critique controlled and directed with a clear purpose
Let the class finish without you
final_quiz.why: An instructor/learner critique should be carefully controlled and organized, not allowed to become a random free-for-all [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: 'In an engine failure after takeoff, do you lower the nose or look for a field?' is which type of question to avoid?
final_quiz.why: Like the AIH's toss-up example, 'should you squawk 7700 or pick a landing spot?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]], it forces a choice between two actions that both belong in a good answer (application).

final_quiz.q: Your usually friendly learner is short-tempered after a rough flight, so you change your tone and choose what to stress and what to leave for later. Which characteristic of effective assessment is this?
final_quiz.why: A flexible assessment fits its tone, technique and content to the occasion and the learner, deciding what to say, omit, stress and minimize [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: On a stage-check prep flight your learner's turns around a point drift badly, and you decide the task needs reteaching. What sequence does the AIH give?
options: Debrief it on the ground and move on to the next lesson as planned
Have the learner practice it solo until it improves
Give a written test on wind drift first
Demonstrate it, let the learner practice it under your direction, then evaluate by watching the performance
final_quiz.why: When an assessment shows a task needs reteaching, the instructor demonstrates the maneuver, lets the learner practice it under direction, and evaluates by observing the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You write a test to see whether your learner is ready for the private pilot knowledge test. What should it be based on?
options: Only the regulations, local area, aircraft type and procedures
The objectives of all the lessons the learner has received
Only the topics the learner finds hardest
A commercial test prep bank, used on its own
final_quiz.why: A test of readiness for the knowledge test should be based on the objectives of all the lessons the learner has received. Regulations, local area, aircraft type and procedures are the objectives of the presolo test [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

final_quiz.q: You suspect your learner flies a perfect slow flight from memory without understanding it. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Have her vary it, combine it with other operations or apply it to other maneuvers
Grade it Perform and move on
Repeat it ten more times the same way
final_quiz.why: Learners who do not understand the principles probably cannot vary the maneuver, combine it with others or apply its elements elsewhere [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

takeaways: Assessment tells both of you where the learner stands and tells you how well you are teaching.
Effective assessment is objective, flexible, acceptable, comprehensive, constructive, organized, thoughtful and specific.
Traditional tests check facts; authentic assessment checks whether the learner can do and decide in the real world.
Let the learner speak first: replay, reconstruct, reflect, redirect, then compare your view with theirs.
Grade maneuvers as describe, explain, practice, perform, and SRM as explain, practice, manage-decide.
Ask brief, one-idea questions that challenge; never 'Do you understand?'
Never sign a solo or practical test endorsement on less than a full, honest check.
cfi_notes: The AIH says a practical test recommendation signed on FAA Form 8710-1 is 'valid for 60 days' [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. 14 CFR 61.39 instead requires the endorsement to certify training received and logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39]], and AC 61-65K restates that 2 calendar month rule [[12:10|AC 61-65K 14]]. Teach the regulation. AC 61-65K separately notes a 60-calendar-day limit, but it applies to finishing a discontinued practical test under 14 CFR 61.43(f) [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.5]].

The learner-centered assessment section refers to 'the scenario that introduced this chapter' [[25:136|AIH 6-5]], but Chapter 6 in this edition opens with no scenario [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. Use the Brian and Linda example on AIH 6-7 instead [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

The AIH grades SRM with explain, practice and manage-decide [[25:137|AIH 6-6]], but the next page says a learner may 'describe' basic SRM on the first flight and its progression example uses describe, practice and manage-decide [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. AIH 1-28 also adds 'not observed' as a fourth SRM grade [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Teach the three-level SRM rubric, use 'not observed' for events not done, and treat 'describe' as informal wording.
FI.I.B already covers evaluation versus critique and knowledge of results. Here, focus on how to deliver and structure the assessment, and point back to that lesson if the examiner asks about timing.

The AIH says flight instructors generally assess with the review, collaborative assessment, written tests and performance-based tests [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], but Chapter 6 never defines a 'review' as an assessment type. Treat it as an informal oral check of earlier material, which matches the oral quizzing purposes listed on AIH 6-11 [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].
For S1, expect the examiner to play a learner who over-rates himself. Run the four R's, then compare ratings calmly, exactly like Linda and Brian [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

Collaborative assessment does not take more time than a normal postflight critique; the AIH calls it a more structured, effective, collaborative version of one [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Use that line if a school worries about debrief length.
Personal minimums are a natural redirect topic. The RMH explains pilots set them more restrictive than the regulations based on experience and proficiency [[30:13|RMH 2-1]].
gaps: The AIH gives no numeric pass mark for flight lessons; the 70 percent figure is only an example criterion objective for a quiz [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Your school's syllabus sets the real standards.
No source gives a fixed number of lessons per rubric level; the describe-practice-manage-decide progression over five flights is only an example [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].
The sources do not give a sample SRM rubric form like Figure 6-4 for risk management; build one from the three SRM grade definitions [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

The Task lists the PHAK and RMH as references, but almost all assessment guidance is in the AIH. The PHAK adds the value of post-flight analysis [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]] and the RMH the PAVE tool [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

Guessing rates for test items (50 percent for true-false, 25 percent for four-option multiple choice) and the matching elimination example are simple arithmetic, not AIH numbers; the AIH only says true-false gives the greatest probability of guessing [[25:198|AIH B-2]] and that equal-column matching invites guessing by elimination [[25:201|AIH B-5]].

activities.title: True or false: traditional tests
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A test item should measure a single objective and call for a single response.
cards.why: True. A test item measures a single objective and calls for a single response [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

cards.s: Discrimination matters more than minimum standards in assessments leading to pilot certification.
cards.why: False. Minimum standards are far more important in assessments leading to pilot certification [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

cards.s: Selection-type items such as multiple choice are easier to grade objectively than essays.
cards.why: True. Selection-type items are much easier to grade objectively [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

cards.s: Traditional assessment never has a place in aviation training.
cards.why: False. It is useful for the factual foundation learners need to reach higher levels of learning [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

cards.s: To estimate validity, several instructors read the test against the stated objectives.
cards.why: True. That is how the AIH says to estimate validity [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

cards.s: Usability is about how well a test separates strong and weak learners.
cards.why: False. Usability is about how easy a test is to give, read and grade; separating learners is discrimination [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

activities.title: Traditional or authentic?
activities.intro: Tap each feature, then tap the kind of assessment it describes.

items.t: Single correct answer for each item
Learner generates a solution instead of choosing one
Usually checks rote and understanding levels
Teaches learners to assess their own work

activities.title: Run the learner-centered debrief
activities.intro: Put the debrief steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Replay: the learner talks through the flight
Reconstruct: what would, could or should have been done differently
Redirect: how it applies to future flights
Compare the learner's self-assessment with yours
Agree on the progress and record it on the rubric

activities.title: Build a criterion-referenced test
activities.intro: Drag each example from the AIH compression test case to the step it belongs to.

pins.label: Describe how to perform a compression test
Answers should mention tools, setup, safety and the steps to get readings
Complete a quiz with a minimum passing score of 70 percent
Write questions covering every area needed to show understanding

activities.title: Scores and guessing
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. All five are application arithmetic built on AIH examples: the 70 percent mark is only the AIH's sample criterion, not an FAA pass mark, and the guessing figures are simple probability, not AIH numbers.

items.q: Application: your compression test quiz uses the AIH's example criterion, a minimum passing score of 70 percent. The quiz has 20 questions. How many must be correct to pass?
items.why: 0.70 x 20 = 14 questions. The 70 percent figure is only the AIH's example criterion objective; your syllabus sets the real standard [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

items.q: Application: an equal-column matching item has 6 terms and 6 answers, each answer used exactly once. A learner truly knows 5 of the pairs. How many can he get right?
items.why: He matches 5, and the sixth answer is the only one left, so he gets it by elimination: 5 + 1 = 6. That is why the AIH says equal-column items should let some answers be used more than once or not at all, and that unequal columns are generally preferable [[25:201|AIH B-5]].

items.q: Application: on that same kind of quiz (70 percent criterion), a learner gets 20 of 30 right. What is the score, to one decimal?
items.why: 20 / 30 x 100 = 66.7 percent, below a 70 percent criterion [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Review every missed item; it shows what was not covered well [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

items.q: Application: a 40-item true-false test. How many would a pure guesser get right on average?
items.why: Each item has two choices: 40 x 1/2 = 20. That is why the AIH says true-false gives the greatest probability of guessing [[25:198|AIH B-2]].

items.q: Application: the same 40 items as four-option multiple choice. How many would a pure guesser get right on average?
items.why: 40 x 1/4 = 10, half the true-false figure. The AIH says three or four alternatives are generally used, that learners are not supposed to guess, and that good distractors attract learners who do not know the answer [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

activities.title: Name the question to avoid
activities.intro: Tap a type, then the example that shows it. Most examples are the AIH's, reworded; the oversize and puzzle ones are new examples in the same style (application).

pairs.r: A long, wandering altimeter question that mixes station pressure, temperature, fronts and mountains
A crosswind, gusty, short-field, partial-flap, rough-engine landing question with one 'first action'
Asking about tire pressure on a test about magneto timing
Answer choices numbered in reverse to catch the learner out

activities.title: Debriefing Leo, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for Leo, a learner pilot with 28 hours, just back from a scenario flight that included steep turns and a simulated engine failure.

steps.s: You sit down for the debrief. How do you start?
options: Read him your list of errors
Ask Leo to replay the flight in his own words
Ask 'Do you think it went well?'
steps.why: Learner-centered assessment begins with the learner's replay of the flight [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. A yes/no question teaches you little [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

steps.s: Leo says his steep turns were perfect. You saw him lose 120 feet in the second one.
options: Tell him he is wrong in front of the dispatcher
Discuss the discrepancy with him at the right moment
steps.why: While the learner replays, listen for inaccurate accounts and discuss the discrepancy at the right moment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Criticize in private [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

steps.s: You coached him twice to hold altitude. Which maneuver grade fits?
steps.why: Practice: he can plan and execute, but your coaching corrected deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

steps.s: In the simulated engine failure, he picked a field only after you asked, 'Where are we going to land?'
steps.why: Explain on the SRM rubric: he knows the risks but needs prompting to identify them and decide [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

steps.s: How do you close the debrief?
options: With specific fixes, what went well, and the plan for next lesson
With a reminder that he could fail his checkride
steps.why: Learners should leave knowing what they did well, what they did poorly and specifically how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. A formative assessment sets the stage for the next lesson [[25:132|AIH 6-1]], and you should try not to end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
